analysis.one_liner: Replaces private health insurance with a government plan covering everyone at no cost-sharing.
analysis.headline: 122 House Democrats cosponsored the Medicare for All Act, but it never received a hearing, markup, or vote in any of its seven assigned committees and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a single national health insurance program run by the Department of Health and Human Services covering every U.S. resident, automatically enrolling people at birth or upon establishing residency. It would cover hospital care, prescriptions, mental health and addiction treatment, dental and vision care, and long-term care, with no deductibles, copays, coinsurance, or balance billing, and no prior-authorization or step-therapy requirements. Private insurers and employers could only sell or provide supplemental coverage on top of the government plan, and the ACA exchanges would shut down once the program was fully running.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident, including the roughly 30 million Americans without insurance and the many more with coverage that leaves them exposed to deductibles and copays. People who today pay premiums, put off care because of cost-sharing, get denied care by insurers, or face medical debt would gain the most: they would get comprehensive coverage with no out-of-pocket charges for covered services and no prior authorization. Older adults, people with disabilities needing long-term care, and families with dental or vision needs would gain benefits they often lack today.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone, especially the uninsured and underinsured

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. resident would be entitled to comprehensive coverage including hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health and substance use treatment, dental and vision services, and long-term care, with automatic enrollment at birth or on establishing residency.
The bill bans all cost-sharing — deductibles, coinsurance, copayments — for covered services, and prohibits providers from balance-billing patients or requiring prior authorization or step therapy.

Private health insurers and employers could only offer coverage that supplements the government plan, not duplicative primary coverage, and the ACA health insurance exchanges would terminate when the program is implemented.
HHS would be required to negotiate prescription drug prices, and hospitals would be paid through global budgets based on Medicare payment rates, aimed at lowering total health spending.

The bill provides transition assistance — wage replacement, retirement benefits, job training, and preferential hiring — for up to five years for workers displaced from health insurance administration jobs.

analysis.who_pays: Whoever funds the Universal Medicare Trust Fund, which would be financed through federal revenue: taxpayers. The bill text creates the trust fund but does not spell out the tax mechanisms, so the financing question would have been settled in the tax-writing committees. Employers now providing coverage would shift from paying premiums to contributing federal taxes. Hospitals and doctors would be paid at Medicare-based rates, generally lower than today's commercial insurance rates, and the private health insurance industry's core business — primary coverage — would be eliminated by law.

drawbacks.text: The bill would require a large increase in federal spending financed by taxes; the trust fund created in the bill does not specify how revenue would be raised, so the burden on individual households would depend on later tax legislation.

Hospital payments would be set through negotiated global budgets anchored to Medicare rates, which are generally below what commercial insurers pay today; supporters argue savings in administration and drug prices offset this, but hospitals — especially financially fragile rural and safety-net ones — could face real adjustment strain.

The transition would eliminate primary-coverage jobs in insurance administration and related functions; the bill acknowledges this by setting aside at least 1 percent of the budget for five years to help displaced workers with wage replacement, retraining, and preferential hiring.

A single-payer program concentrates enormous power over covered benefits, payment rates, and national coverage determinations in one federal agency; the bill provides appeals processes, practice-guideline overrides for treating clinicians, and an ombudsman, but opponents argue this reduces choice and flexibility compared with competing private plans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is the largest available in health policy: universal, comprehensive coverage with zero cost-sharing, covering benefits like long-term care, dental, and vision that most Americans today buy separately or go without. The cost is equally large: a major new federal financing obligation whose tax incidence the bill leaves to future legislation, plus payment-rate cuts for providers and the deliberate elimination of the private primary-insurance market. Whether it was net-positive for households depends on how the financing was structured — moderate-income families who today pay premiums and deductibles would very likely come out ahead; higher-income households would likely pay more in taxes than they save. The design is detailed on the delivery side (global budgets, provider ethics rules, whistleblower protections) but thin on the financing side, which is where its political fate would have been decided.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to seven House committees and two subcommittees, and the record shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened — it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Jayapal introduced the Medicare for All Act of 2021 on March 17, 2021, with more than 100 original Democratic cosponsors named in the bill's introduction.

The Speaker referred it to seven committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Rules, Oversight and Reform, Armed Services, and Judiciary — and it was subsequently sent to the Health Subcommittee and the Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security Subcommittee.
After the subcommittee referrals, the record shows no further action: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2023.
All 122 cosponsors were Democrats; not a single House Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, pharmaceutical companies, and employers that would have lost their role in financing and administering primary health coverage all kept the status quo intact. House members who preferred not to vote on the record also avoided a politically difficult roll call. Americans without adequate coverage gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers, drug makers, and employers

for.name: Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare for All Act of 2021 and recruited a large bloc of House Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 122 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the chairs of key committees; the cosponsor list includes no Republicans.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action to advance the bill after referral; no markup or committee vote occurred.

against.name: House Republican conference
against.what_they_did: Opposed government-run universal health coverage; not one House Republican cosponsored the bill.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Private health insurers (led by trade group America's Health Insurance Plans)
against.what_they_did: Ran a public campaign against single-payer proposals, which would have eliminated private primary health coverage by law.

sides.party_line_note: All 122 cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans, but even with a Democratic House majority and a Democratic president, the bill never reached a vote in any committee or on the floor.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful for private insurers to sell coverage duplicating the government plan, ending their core business of primary coverage; they could only sell supplemental coverage. Insurers profit from premiums, deductibles, and utilization management that the bill would abolish, so their interest ran directly against the bill's beneficiaries.
HHS would be required to negotiate drug prices under a national health budget, threatening current pricing power. Drug prices are a major driver of what patients pay out of pocket today.

Hospitals would get predictable quarterly global-budget payments instead of billing dozens of insurers, cutting their administrative costs, but payment would be anchored to Medicare rates below commercial levels and compensation caps would apply to executives. A single-payer program also guarantees universal payment for care that currently goes uncompensated for the uninsured.

Employers would be freed from paying most health premiums but would contribute through federal financing, and would be barred from providing duplicative primary coverage — losing a benefit they use to recruit and retain workers, while gaining a healthier, portable-insured workforce.
Jobs built around underwriting, claims processing, and plan sales would shrink sharply; the bill specifically funds wage replacement and retraining for these displaced workers for up to five years.
